notes: Seed set. Coordinates are approximate, taken from street intersections, and must be checked against Sanborn maps. Teasers are written in our own words; the full story lives at each source link. Photo image URLs follow the OpenSFHistory pattern and have not been fetched from the build machine, so check they load. Status is draft or published; only published stories show in the app.

stories.title: The ballpark beside the park
stories.teaser: A semi pro ballpark filled this block next to Golden Gate Park, with cable cars running to the gate and a saloon tucked under the grandstands. About 10,000 people came for opening day in 1887. The first Stanford and California Big Games were played here before the land was sold for houses.

photos.caption: A game between the Haverlys and the Pioneers at the Haight Street Grounds
photos.credit: J. A. Todd, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp33.00518

photos.caption: Cable cars at Haight and Stanyan, by the old ballpark entrance
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp13.234

stories.verification_notes: Location per the 1889 Sanborn map as described by SF Story: Stanyan between Frederick and Waller; Wikipedia says bounded by Stanyan, Waller, Shrader and Frederick. The Big Game claim comes from Wikipedia only.

stories.title: Shoot the Chutes on Haight Street
stories.teaser: A block from the park stood the Chutes, an amusement ground whose star ride sent riders down a steep slide into an artificial lake. It added a roller coaster, a zoo and a vaudeville theater, then moved to Fulton Street in 1902 and later to Fillmore and Playland.

source.title: Architecture Spotlight: Chutes in the Haight
source.author: Untapped Cities

photos.caption: The waterslide at the Haight Chutes on opening day
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.1133

stories.verification_notes: Between Clayton and Cole on Haight per Untapped Cities. Add a second source and an OpenSFHistory photo. OpenSFHistory describes the site as bounded by Haight, Waller, Cole and Clayton, and places it at 37.7692, -122.4504. A second text source is still wanted.

stories.title: From movie house to rock dances
stories.teaser: A neighborhood movie theater opened on this corner in 1910 and later grew to about 1,500 seats. After it stopped showing films in 1964 it became the Straight Theater, a home for 1960s rock dances. The building was torn down in the late 1970s and a Goodwill stands here now.

photos.caption: The closed Haight Theatre at Haight and Cole before its summer 1979 demolition
photos.credit: Greg Gaar, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp67.0095

photos.caption: Haight Theatre ad for August 2, 1914
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp67.0039

stories.verification_notes: 1702 Haight at Cole. Demolition is given as August 1979 in the main article and 1981 in comments; confirm. Dates and events of the Straight Theater period (1966 to 1967) need a second source such as the Straight Theater history site. The OpenSFHistory caption for the May 1979 photo says the theatre was demolished in summer 1979, which supports the 1979 date over 1981.

stories.title: The Psychedelic Shop
stories.teaser: Brothers Jay and Ron Thelin opened a head shop at 1535 Haight Street in January 1966, selling incense, posters, records and clothing. It became a gathering place for the counterculture. They closed it for good on October 6, 1967, the day of the Death of Hippie ceremony, and gave away what was left.

source.title: This Day in Cannabis History: the Psychedelic Shop
source.author: World of Cannabis Museum

stories.verification_notes: Address from the museum page; the exact spot on the block needs checking. The Death of Hippie date (Oct 6, 1967, Buena Vista Park) comes from Wikipedia's Haight-Ashbury article. Find a stronger historical source.

stories.title: The comedy club at Carl and Cole
stories.teaser: In the 1980s The Other Cafe at 100 Carl Street became a full time comedy club and an early stage for comics including Robin Williams, Dana Carvey and Whoopi Goldberg. The corner now holds a crepe restaurant.
stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Confirm the performers and that the tenant is still Crepes on Cole. Look for a Western Neighborhoods Project or newspaper source.

stories.title: The college that became a hospital
stories.teaser: Doctors and students from the Affiliated Colleges on this slope helped run relief care after the 1906 earthquake, while the Army ran a field hospital in Golden Gate Park. The disaster pushed a planned teaching hospital to the top of the list, and the first UC Hospital opened here in April 1907.

source.title: 1906 earthquake spurs rapid response at Parnassus
source.author: UCSF

stories.verification_notes: UCSF Library's history site (history.library.ucsf.edu) has period photos with open reuse notes; add one.

more.title: Streetwise: Hospitals in the Western Neighborhoods
Streetwise: Time It Was

stories.title: The world's fair in the park
stories.teaser: In 1894 a fair of about 200 acres filled the park around today's Music Concourse, with roughly 120 buildings and more than two million visitors. Most of it was taken down afterward, but the Japanese Tea Garden and the Concourse were kept.

source.title: 125 years ago: Midwinter International Exposition in Golden Gate Park
source.author: Richmond Review and Sunset Beacon

photos.caption: Crowd at the first shovelful of sand for the Midwinter Fair site
photos.credit: Isaiah West Taber, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.01330

photos.caption: The Bonet Electric Tower at the Midwinter Fair
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.075

stories.verification_notes: Opening day photo is by Isaiah West Taber via the Western Neighborhoods Project; find its OpenSFHistory id.

more.title: Streetwise: Fountains of the Western Neighborhoods

stories.title: The streetcar graveyard
stories.teaser: This whole block between Irving, Lincoln Way, 14th and Funston was once a yard where retired streetcars waited for the scrapper among the Sunset sand. It was planned as a carhouse in 1907 and later served Muni as a storage lot.

photos.caption: Aerial view of the streetcar boneyard, looking west on Irving at 14th Avenue
photos.credit: Via SFMTA blog; original source to confirm

stories.verification_notes: The SFMTA post points to a Western Neighborhoods Project article and podcast episode 182; make that the primary source.

stories.title: Many lives of a corner
stories.teaser: In the early 1970s the southeast corner of Ninth and Irving held a bar called The Stein, also known as Mac's Place, with green streetcars rattling past. A Jamba Juice came later, and a French chicken sandwich restaurant was announced for the space in 2025.

source.title: Then and Now: Ninth Avenue and Irving Street
source.author: Richmond Review and Sunset Beacon

photos.caption: Ninth Avenue and Irving Street with a dentist above a pharmacy
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.11201

photos.caption: Mac's Place, The Stein, on the southeast corner of Ninth Avenue and Irving Street (postcard)
photos.credit: Private collector / Western Neighborhoods Project / OpenSFHistory

photos.caption: 9th Avenue and Irving Street
photos.credit: John Harder, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.50234

photos.caption: 9th Avenue and Irving Street
photos.credit: Richmond Review Newspaper Collection, courtesy of Paul Kozakiewicz, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp07.00067

stories.verification_notes: Check whether the French restaurant opened as announced before showing the last sentence. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

more.title: Streetwise: Take Two Aspirin in the Western Neighborhoods
Streetwise: Dining on the West Side

stories.title: The bakery's earlier self
stories.teaser: In November 1904 this Ninth Avenue building, between Irving and Judah, looked very different from the busy bakery it holds today at 1331 Ninth Avenue. A photo from the neighborhood archive shows it in its early days.

source.title: Historical Photo: Popular Inner Sunset shop long before customer lines
source.author: Richmond Review and Sunset Beacon

photos.caption: 9th Avenue near Irving, the site of today's Arizmendi Bakery
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.4162

photos.caption: The Ninth Avenue building between Irving and Judah, November 1904
photos.credit: Private collector / Western Neighborhoods Project / OpenSFHistory

stories.verification_notes: Light entry. Find the story of the building's first occupant before publishing.

stories.title: The orphanage on the dunes
stories.teaser: In 1905 a purpose built brick home for children opened here, out among the sand dunes. Seven months later the 1906 earthquake wrecked it, yet every one of the 59 children inside got out unhurt. They camped on the dunes for twelve days.

photos.caption: The Nursery for Homeless Children on the north side of Lake Street between 14th and 15th Avenues
photos.credit: San Francisco Public Library, AAD-5883

stories.verification_notes: A 1906 newspaper transcription places the Nursery at 13th and Lake; annual reports and SF Story say 14th. Confirm on the Sanborn map.

stories.title: The orphanage that fell apart
stories.teaser: A few blocks east stood the Maria Kip Orphanage, which a 1906 report called the most complete ruin among the city's children's homes. All 125 children inside at the moment of the quake survived.

source.title: Every institution in the city for care of children damaged
source.author: 1906 newspaper account, transcribed
source.publisher: Museum of the City of San Francisco

photos.caption: The Maria Kip Orphanage, Lake Street near 7th Avenue, damaged after the 1906 earthquake
photos.credit: Harry O. Wood, Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley, BANC PIC 1957.007 Ser.1:115

stories.verification_notes: Confirm the 125 figure and the building's later fate in a second source.

stories.title: The farm at the edge of the Presidio
stories.teaser: Before the avenues filled in, a small farm ran along the Presidio boundary here. The Bauchou family lived at 9 14th Avenue, and in 1905 they were the new orphanage's nearest neighbors, with Mountain Lake visible down the slope.

photos.caption: Bauchou home on 14th Avenue, view east toward Mountain Lake
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.207

stories.verification_notes: OpenSFHistory caption names Bernard Bauchou as the occupant of 9 14th Avenue.

stories.title: The refugee shack that started a movement
stories.teaser: Behind a plain Sunset facade stand three 1906 relief cottages joined together, with a fourth in the backyard. Jane Cryan moved in during 1982, learned what they were and fought for them. In 1984 the city landmarked the house, the only refugee shack it has ever protected.

source.title: This tiny SF shack tipped off a decades long preservation movement
source.author: Keith Menconi

stories.verification_notes: Address 1227 24th Avenue and Landmark No. 171 per the Examiner; Atlas Obscura confirms Cryan's 1982 lease and Landmark 171. The 1984 landmark year comes from the Examiner only. Pin placed on the block, not the lot.

stories.title: Iceland on 48th Avenue
stories.teaser: Inside an ordinary Outer Sunset block, a barn like building held a full size ice rink from 1926. Kids learned to skate and played junior hockey while the surf rolled a few streets away. Insurance costs and decay ended it, and the rink came down in 1991 for condominiums.

photos.caption: Interior of the San Francisco Ice Arena
photos.credit: Greg Gaar, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp72.16436

stories.verification_notes: Address 1557 48th Avenue per SF Story; opened March 1926, demolished July 8, 1991. Pin placed on the block.

stories.title: The castle on Strawberry Hill
stories.teaser: A reddish concrete lookout with little bastion towers once crowned Strawberry Hill, the park's highest point, paid for by Thomas Sweeny. Carriages rolled up for the panorama and a waterfall tumbled toward Stow Lake. The 1906 earthquake wrecked it, and parts of the foundation remain today.

photos.caption: Sweeny's Observatory on Strawberry Hill
photos.credit: Isaiah West Taber, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.397

photos.caption: The observatory in ruins after the earthquake
photos.credit: James Stoddard, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.5474

photos.caption: Sweeny Observatory after the earthquake
photos.credit: Marilyn Blaisdell Collection, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.03760

stories.verification_notes: Dedicated Sept 19, 1891 and ruined April 18, 1906 per SF Story. Pin set on Strawberry Hill summit; remains are near it. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

more.title: Streetwise: Post Earthquake Scenes in the Western Neighborhoods

stories.title: The janitor who ran the saloon
stories.teaser: In 1895 a roadhouse nicknamed the Milk Punch House stood beside the Laguna Honda School on Seventh Avenue. Its owner, Irish born Elizabeth Chadwick, also worked as the school janitor while raising three children upstairs. A grand jury objected, the school board argued for months and parents signed petitions in her defense.

photos.caption: The Laguna Honda School, damaged in 1906, with the saloon beside it
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.1265

stories.verification_notes: School stood on 7th Avenue between Irving and Judah, saloon just north of it, per SF Story. The article does not say whether the saloon building survives.

stories.title: A house on the dunes, still standing
stories.teaser: House painter Elbert Dodge bought four lots on bare dunes in 1903 and spent a year of Sundays and holidays building a home with his brother. He added strawberries, fruit trees, chickens and a windmill well. The Chronicle admired him in 1905, and the house still stands on 22nd Avenue.
stories.verification_notes: Address 1549 22nd Avenue per SF Story. Pin placed on the block. Private home, view from the street.

stories.title: The day a twister took a Sunset house
stories.teaser: On February 24, 1930, a storm shoved a lone house at 46th Avenue and Ortega off its foundation and left it leaning in the sand. Police first heard reports of an explosion. Owner John Volz was at work, lost about 5,000 dollars and rebuilt with a ground floor garage.

photos.caption: The house knocked off its foundation after the storm
photos.credit: Emiliano Echeverria, Randolph Brandt Collection, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp30.0124

stories.verification_notes: Address 1896 46th Avenue per SF Story, which also corrects newspaper claims that the house spun 90 degrees.

stories.title: A flight school on the sand
stories.teaser: In 1914 the Christofferson brothers taught flying on the sand at the foot of Sloat Boulevard, just as the Great Highway was being built. Their daredevil circle was short lived. Several of the pilots tied to the school, including Silas Christofferson in 1916, were killed in crashes within a few years.
stories.verification_notes: Location described as at the foot of Sloat Boulevard near the Great Highway; the exact hangar site is not given, so the pin is approximate. No archive photo IDs listed in the article.

stories.title: The hog ranch at 14th and Lincoln
stories.teaser: Cornelius Reynolds, an English immigrant, claimed dunes near today's 14th Avenue and Lincoln Way in the 1860s and raised hogs, then ran a small saloon. Family deaths came one after another. After 1906 he sold land to the streetcar company. Apartments now cover the ranch, though its old boundary still shows.

photos.caption: View from Strawberry Hill over the western dunes
photos.credit: Charles Turrill, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.4937

photos.caption: The Inner Sunset seen from Mount Sutro
photos.credit: W. C. Billington, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.569

stories.verification_notes: Ranch location per SF Story: 14th Avenue and Lincoln Way (then H Street). Sits near our streetcar boneyard card; the two stories overlap on the same block.

stories.title: Making 19th Avenue
stories.teaser: Around 1900 19th Avenue was mostly a line on a map, with Carl Larsen's chicken ranch near today's Noriega and Ortega. A rutted track was paved by 1916, and a 1929 right of way near Lake Merced let it connect south. After the Golden Gate Bridge, it was widened into Highway 1.

photos.caption: View north from Moraga Street over the dunes
photos.credit: Charles Turrill, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.713

photos.caption: Fresh paving near Quintara Street
photos.credit: Horace Chaffee, Department of Public Works, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp36.01322

stories.verification_notes: Larsen ranch between Noriega and Ortega per SF Story; the pin is placed there.

stories.title: The Mothers Building
stories.teaser: Herbert and Mortimer Fleishhacker gave this Italian Renaissance rest house in 1925 in memory of their mother, a refuge for mothers and children beside the zoo. Women artists added Noah's Ark murals in the 1930s. It closed in 2002 as unsafe and still waits for repairs.

photos.caption: The new Mothers Building and wading pool
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.1412

photos.caption: Children at the wading pool
photos.credit: Gabriel Moulin, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.4762

photos.caption: The Mothers Building
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.11465

stories.verification_notes: Architect George Kelham; city landmark 2022. Inside the zoo grounds, so the building is only visible from zoo property. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

Streetwise: Looking Back 100 Years Ago in the Western Neighborhoods

stories.title: The last roadhouse
stories.teaser: Hidden behind redwoods below 19th Avenue, the Trocadero opened in 1892 as a roadhouse known for turtle soup. Political boss Abe Ruef was arrested here in 1907. It later served as a women's outdoor club. A falling eucalyptus smashed the roof in 2023, and restoration finished in 2025.

photos.caption: Postcard advertisement for the Trocadero
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.03678

photos.caption: View past the turtle pond
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.1604

stories.verification_notes: City landmark 301 (April 5, 2022) per SF Story. Pin placed on the slope in Stern Grove below 19th Avenue.

stories.title: Parkside on the dunes
stories.teaser: The first Parkside homes rose on dunes near Vicente and 32nd Avenue in 1907, sold by the Parkside Realty Company. Residents formed an improvement club in 1908 to demand services, and Eugene Williams opened the district's first grocery in 1909. The L Taraval streetcar arrived in 1923.
stories.verification_notes: Commercial hub at Taraval and 32nd Avenue per SF Story; the first homes were slightly south, so the pin is approximate. The article also covers discriminatory covenants of the era.

stories.title: A steam engine on the zoo playground
stories.teaser: In August 1957 Southern Pacific donated switch engine 1294 to the zoo playground. A crane company moved it for free, local Teamsters paid for climbing bars, and children rang its bell for decades. Fog corroded the engine, and it was removed and scrapped around 1981.

photos.caption: The engine surprises the crowd on moving day
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.2963

photos.caption: The engine backs into the playground
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.2964

stories.verification_notes: Dedicated Nov 29, 1957. The article gives both early 1980s removal and 1981 scrapping, so the end date is stated loosely.

more.title: Streetwise: Summertime in the Western Neighborhoods

stories.title: The biggest pool in America
stories.teaser: Opened in 1925 beside the Great Highway, Fleishhacker Pool was billed as the largest swimming pool in the United States, 1,000 feet long and filled with seawater. Lifeguards patrolled in rowboats. Storm damage to a pipe in 1971 doomed it, and it was filled in and turned into zoo parking.

photos.caption: View south toward the Fleishhacker Pool site from the foot of Sloat Boulevard
photos.credit: Horace Chaffee, SF Department of Public Works, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp36.02798

photos.caption: Fleishhacker Pool shortly after opening
photos.credit: Horace Chaffee, SF Department of Public Works, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp36.03225

photos.caption: Fleishhacker Pool
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.4724

stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia, read Oct 21, 2026). Pool house burned December 1, 2012. Pin on the former pool site, now parking; exact outline not checked. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

stories.title: Opening day for the Sunset Tunnel
stories.teaser: On October 21, 1928, thousands came to the western portal at Carl and Cole to watch Mayor Sunny Jim Rolph pilot a streetcar through the new tunnel. The line to the ocean made the Sunset practical to live in. Digging had begun in 1926 and cost about 1.5 million dollars.

photos.caption: Mayor James Rolph at the controls of the first N line streetcar through the tunnel, near Carl and Cole
photos.credit: Horace Chaffee, SF Department of Public Works, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.0493

photos.caption: Tunnel construction on Carl near Cole
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.496

photos.caption: A cake shaped like the Duboce Avenue entrance of the Sunset Tunnel
photos.credit: Horace Chaffee, SF Department of Public Works, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp36.03581

stories.verification_notes: Opening day facts from SFMTA; groundbreaking June 10, 1926 and cost $1,477,618 from Wikipedia's Sunset Tunnel page. Pin moved to OpenSFHistory's map point for the dedication photo. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

more.title: Streetwise: October Happenings in the Western Neighborhoods

stories.title: Kezar Stadium
stories.teaser: Willis Polk's stadium opened in Golden Gate Park in 1925 and later became the first home of the 49ers, who played here until 1970. Nearly 60,000 seats held the crowds. It hosted concerts afterward, and the original stadium was torn down in 1989 for a smaller rebuild.

source.title: Kezar Stadium: San Francisco's Pro Football Roots
source.author: Jeremy Menzies

photos.caption: A man works on seating during construction of Kezar Stadium
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.0039

photos.caption: Crowds fill the stands for the 1950 Shrine East West Game
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp25.5346

stories.verification_notes: Dates cross checked with Wikipedia (dedication May 2, 1925; demolition and rebuild 1989). Architect credit is SFMTA's. Pin moved to the OpenSFHistory map point for Kezar photos.

more.title: Streetwise: Autumn Days in the Western Neighborhoods

stories.title: From almshouse to hospital
stories.teaser: Laguna Honda began in 1867 as an almshouse for the poor and sick, on 87 acres where residents grew food and kept dairy cows. After the 1906 earthquake a 1,000 bed wing opened and was dedicated in 1909 by Theodore Roosevelt. The Spanish Revival main buildings followed in 1926.

photos.caption: The almshouse on the future site of Laguna Honda Hospital
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.777

photos.caption: Laguna Honda Hospital with Mount Sutro and Twin Peaks behind
photos.credit: Turrill & Miller, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.7885

stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Coordinates from the article's infobox.

more.title: Streetwise: Hospitals in the Western Neighborhoods

stories.title: The arboretum that waited fifty years
stories.teaser: John McLaren sketched plans for an arboretum in the 1880s, but money never came. Then Helene Strybing left a bequest in 1927. WPA workers began planting in 1937 and the arboretum opened in May 1940. Today it is the San Francisco Botanical Garden, entered at Ninth Avenue and Lincoln.
stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Pin on the Ninth Avenue gate area.

stories.title: The tower people loved to hate
stories.teaser: When Sutro Tower went up in 1973, many neighbors hated it. Columnist Herb Caen joked it would stalk down the hill and attack the Golden Gate Bridge. Lights on its legs were removed after public outcry. It gathered TV transmitters that had been scattered across Bay Area hilltops.
stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Completed July 4, 1973. Tower sits on Clarendon Heights just above Cole Valley and the Inner Sunset.

stories.title: The streetcar that ate the dunes
stories.teaser: In 1910 the United Railroads built a special streetcar that scooped sand from the dunes around 21st Avenue and Ortega Street and loaded it onto work cars. Sand gives steel wheels grip on rails. Muni still sands its vehicles, but the dunes were long ago built over.
stories.verification_notes: Location and 1910 date from the SFMTA caption. Photos are in the SFMTA archive; no OpenSFHistory ID given.

stories.title: The L Taraval begins
stories.teaser: On April 12, 1919, small streetcars began shuttling from West Portal to Taraval and 33rd Avenue, Muni's thirteenth line. Riders transferred to the K to reach downtown. Tracks reached 48th Avenue in 1923, and a WPA extension in 1937 brought the line to 46th and Wawona, serving the zoo and pool.

source.title: Dunes to Destinations: 100 Years on the L Taraval
source.author: Jeremy Menzies

photos.caption: L line Magic Carpet car 1005 on Taraval near 23rd Avenue
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.50416

photos.caption: An L line car passes the Richfield station at Taraval and 28th Avenue
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.1507

stories.verification_notes: Dates from the SFMTA article. Pin at the original Taraval and 33rd terminal.

stories.title: The velodrome at Baker and Fell
stories.teaser: A banana shaped bicycle track and grandstand opened at Baker and Fell on November 21, 1896. Too few paying fans came, so promoters tried rugby, push ball and fireworks. The last races ran on October 3, 1897, and the track went to East Oakland. Later Southern Pacific built a hospital here.

photos.caption: View from Buena Vista Park north to the Panhandle and the velodrome
photos.credit: D. H. Wulzen, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp13.032

photos.caption: The Southern Pacific Hospital at Fell and Baker
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.02742

stories.verification_notes: Northwest corner of Baker and Fell per SF Story. The article does not say what is on the block today.

stories.title: Ground zero at Haight and Ashbury
stories.teaser: This Colonial Revival corner building at Haight and Ashbury was raised in 1907 to add storefronts. In the 1960s it housed an early hippie boutique, Mnasidika, at 1510 Haight, and is tied to Janis Joplin and the Grateful Dead. The city made it a landmark in 2006.

source.title: San Francisco Historic Landmark: Doolan-Larson Residence and Storefronts
source.author: NoeHill

stories.verification_notes: Landmark 253 approved July 14, 2006 per NoeHill; Wikipedia's Haight-Ashbury article adds the National Register listing. The Joplin and Dead links are loose and not detailed in the source.

stories.title: The funeral of the hippie
stories.teaser: On October 6, 1967, the Diggers carried a coffin down Haight Street to mark the death of the hippie. Mourners burned underground papers and clothes and knelt at Haight and Ashbury. The aim was to end media hype and the selling of the movement after the Summer of Love.

source.title: Death of Hippie: An end to the Summer of Love
source.author: UC Santa Cruz Library

stories.verification_notes: Funeral notice named Buena Vista Park; the procession ran down Haight Street per the exhibit. Wikipedia places the staged funeral at Buena Vista Park. Pin set at the kneel in corner.

stories.title: The first free clinic
stories.teaser: As tens of thousands of young people poured into the Haight in the Summer of Love, Dr. David Smith opened a free clinic on June 7, 1967. It became the model for hundreds more across the country. Bill Graham's benefit concerts helped keep it open until it closed in 2019.
stories.verification_notes: Opening date confirmed by Wikipedia and 730stanyan.org. Street address was NOT confirmed in a fetched source, so the pin is only the general area of Haight and Clayton. Check before sharing.

stories.title: The city's oldest library building
stories.teaser: Opened on October 29, 1909 at 1833 Page Street, the Park Branch was the first San Francisco branch built with public money. The McDougall Brothers designed it. A mural went up in 1975 and a renovation finished in 2011, though the 1989 earthquake cost it its circular skylights.
stories.verification_notes: Address per SF Story; pin is approximate along Page Street. Photos exist at SFPL (AAC-5839, AAC-5848) but no stable page URL was checked.

stories.title: A library on an empty block
stories.teaser: When the Sunset Branch Library opened on March 25, 1918, it stood alone on its block at Irving and 19th Avenue, built for under 44,000 dollars. The site had been an old barn that neighbors disliked because boys used it for target practice. Jefferson Elementary now fills the lot beside it.

source.title: Then and Now: Irving Street at 19th Avenue
source.author: Sunset Beacon

photos.caption: Irving Street at 19th Avenue, a few years before the library opened
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.1833

photos.caption: Children in soldier costumes on the library grounds at 19th and Irving
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.1994

stories.verification_notes: Opening date and cost per the Sunset Beacon caption of a 1920 photo.

stories.title: A streetcar meets a tar truck
stories.teaser: Around 1940 a streetcar collided with a roofing tar truck at Fourth Avenue and Irving Street, a sticky scene someone photographed. The Sunset Beacon matched it with a modern view from the same spot, where trees and a UCSF building now stand and the parking has changed.

source.title: Then and Now: Fourth Avenue and Irving Street
source.author: Sunset Beacon

stories.verification_notes: Thin: a single photo caption. Included as a light event card.

stories.title: 710 Ashbury
stories.teaser: Members of the Grateful Dead shared this house at 710 Ashbury Street in the mid 1960s. In 1967 police arrested band members here for drug possession. The band answered with a press conference on the premises, arguing marijuana should be decriminalized and that local police were singling them out.
stories.verification_notes: HELD AS DRAFT: single tertiary source (Clio, citing Lonely Planet). Its own dates conflict (1965 to 1968 versus 1967). Needs a second source.

stories.title: The Red House on Haight
stories.teaser: Jimi Hendrix is believed to have lived for a time in an apartment above a shop at 1524A Haight Street, a few doors from the main intersection. The building is painted red in his honor, which gives it the name Red House. It is a private residence, so look from the street.
stories.verification_notes: HELD AS DRAFT: the source says details of his stay are sparse and uses hedged language. Needs a second source.

stories.title: The tunnel that survived 1906
stories.teaser: Ernest Ransome built this small arch in 1889 so people could walk from Alvord Lake to the children's playground without crossing the carriage drive. It is believed to be the first reinforced concrete bridge in the United States. Sculpted stalactites give the underpass a cave look, and it came through 1906 undamaged.

photos.caption: Inside the Alvord Lake Bridge with its original concrete stalactites
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp33.03911

stories.verification_notes: Suggested by David. Cross checked with Wikipedia, ASCE and a Richmond Sunset News piece (2022-08-03) and the OpenSFHistory 'Bridges of Golden Gate Park' post. Sources differ on the span (20 ft versus 29 ft) and on the ASCE landmark year (1969 versus a plaque on July 18, 1970), so neither is stated. The 'first' claim is hedged because ASCE's own text says 'believed'.

stories.title: America's first public playground?
stories.teaser: Opened in 1888 as the Sharon Quarters for Children, this Golden Gate Park playground is often called the first public playground in the United States. An 1894 photo already shows a carousel, swings and the Sharon Building for rainy days. The concrete slide survived a 2007 renovation that added the Koret name.

source.title: Koret Children's Quarter and Carousel
source.author: San Francisco Recreation and Park Department

photos.caption: Carousel, Sharon Building, swings and children at the Children's Playground
photos.credit: Isaiah West Taber, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.357

photos.caption: The gondola swing at the Children's Playground
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.0053

photos.caption: The Sharon Building at the Children's Playground after earthquake damage
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp33.04022

stories.verification_notes: Suggested by David. The 1888 opening and 'first' claim appear on the Rec and Park page ('thought to be') and on 730stanyan.org. The 'first' claim is treated as traditional, not proven. The current carousel is a 1914 Herschell Spillman installed in 1940, so the 1894 carousel is a different one. Pin from the archive's map point for the 1894 photo. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

stories.title: The goat cart men of the Children's Playground
stories.teaser: For a coin, children could ride a little wicker cart pulled by a harnessed goat in the Children's Playground, a treat that also ran at Woodward's Gardens in the Mission. The city ended the attraction in the 1930s and sold twelve carts and six harnesses to a toy shop owner for ten dollars.

photos.caption: Goat drawn carts, people on a bench and a baby carriage, probably at the Children's Playground
photos.credit: J. F. Jarvis, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp24.345a

photos.caption: A child in a goat cart with two more children, Children's Playground
photos.credit: Photographer unknown, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.2853

stories.verification_notes: SF Story read in full. Pin from the archive map point for wnp24.345a, offset slightly from the Koret entry. The Golden Gate Park location rests on the photo caption and SF Story's mention of the Children's Playground.

stories.title: The 272 foot tower that lit up the Midwinter Fair
stories.teaser: Rising 272 feet above what is now the Music Concourse, Leopold Bonet's Electric Tower opened with the 1894 Midwinter Fair, glittering with over 3,000 lights and a giant searchlight. The concession never paid. In January 1896 dynamite finally toppled it after ropes and earlier explosives failed.

photos.caption: Elevated view east over the opening day parade, with Bonet's Electric Tower at left
photos.credit: Isaiah West Taber, Marilyn Blaisdell Collection, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.03101

photos.caption: The fallen tower on its side in the Music Concourse, awaiting scrapping
photos.credit: Photographer unknown, Marilyn Blaisdell Collection, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.03263

stories.verification_notes: SF Story read in full. Demolition dates: attempt January 11, 1896, final blast the following Sunday (apparently January 12). Pin from archive map point; tower footprint not checked against fair plans.

stories.title: A bicycle stadium that became the Be-In field
stories.teaser: The Polo Fields opened on July 4, 1906 as a bicycle racing stadium and only became a polo field in 1931. In 1911 President Taft broke ground here for the Panama Pacific fair, which was later built in the Marina. In 1967 the grass hosted the Human Be-In.

photos.caption: President Taft breaks ground for the Panama Pacific International Exposition at its first planned site, the Golden Gate Park Polo Fields
photos.credit: Emiliano Echeverria and Randolph Brandt Collection, courtesy of Emiliano Echeverria, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp30.0003

stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia, read Oct 22, 2026). A 1961 Rosary rally was suggested by an earlier search but is not in this source, so it is left out until a second source is found. The 1911 Taft groundbreaking is from the WNP October 2024 Streetwise column and is consistent with the archive caption for wnp33.00934; the fair was moved to the Marina District. Pin from that photo's map point. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

more.title: Streetwise: October Happenings in the Western Neighborhoods

stories.title: Thirty nine redwoods for thirty nine sons
stories.teaser: In 1920 the Native Sons and Native Daughters planted 39 acacias on Junipero Serra Boulevard, one for each local member lost in World War I. In 1927 the grove was dedicated again as 39 redwoods in Golden Gate Park, and a standing Doughboy statue by M. Earl Cummings joined it in 1930.

photos.caption: The Doughboy by M. Earl Cummings at the Grove of Memory
photos.credit: Photographer unknown, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.2791

photos.caption: Junipero Serra Boulevard near Ocean Avenue, site of the original grove
photos.credit: Photographer unknown, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.0149

stories.verification_notes: SF Story read in full; the page gives no author or date. Pin from the archive map point for the 1930 Doughboy photo. The 1926 photo shows the original Junipero Serra site, which is a different location.

stories.title: A medical school in the sand dunes
stories.teaser: In 1895 Mayor Adolph Sutro gave the University of California 13 acres on windswept Mount Parnassus. A cornerstone went down in March 1897, and critics mourned a medical school buried in sand dunes. By October 1898 three Romanesque buildings stood where mule drawn scoops had levelled the ground.

source.title: How UCSF's Historic Parnassus Heights Campus Rose from Remote Sand Dunes
source.author: Eric Brooks

stories.verification_notes: Read in full. Cornerstone laid March 27, 1897; time capsule opened 1967. No archive photo identified yet. Pin placed at Parnassus Heights, not at the original building footprint.

Streetwise: Time It Was

stories.title: The park's emergency hospital
stories.teaser: Designed by city architect Newton Tharp and built in 1902, Park Emergency Hospital was San Francisco's first permanent emergency hospital. The 1906 earthquake collapsed its entrance, doctors worked in tents nearby, and it was rebuilt with stone from fallen downtown buildings. It closed as a hospital in 1978 and appears in Dirty Harry.

source.title: The Very Old Hospital in Golden Gate Park
source.author: Curbed SF

stories.verification_notes: Read in full. Landmark No. 201, 1991. The page places it in the Kezar parking lot; the address 811 Stanyan comes from an image filename and the search result, so treat the address as unconfirmed. Pin approximate. No author named on the reposted page.

stories.title: Maud's, the lesbian bar on Cole Street
stories.teaser: From 1966 until its last drink on September 9, 1989, Maud's at 937 Cole Street was a refuge founded by Rikki Streicher. Janis Joplin, Del Martin and Phyllis Lyon were patrons, and its softball team played in the gay league. In 2025 supervisors began making the surviving building a landmark.

source.title: Resolution No. 485-25, initiating landmark designation of Maud's
source.author: San Francisco Board of Supervisors
source.publisher: City and County of San Francisco

stories.verification_notes: Two sources agree: the Board resolution (929 to 941 Cole parcel, 937 Cole bar, closed 1989, Landmark process begun Oct 21, 2025) and Wikipedia (opened 1966 as The Study, last drink Sept 9, 1989). The resolution says only 'mid 1960s' for opening. Documentary Last Call at Maud's was released in 1993. Pin approximate for the 900 block of Cole.

stories.title: The Chautauqua House
stories.teaser: From 1967 to 1986 this 1909 house at 1451 Masonic Avenue was home to the American Indian Historical Society, founded by Rupert and Jeannette Costo and others. It published The Indian Historian, held gallery space, and hosted Richard Oakes's education committee as the Alcatraz occupation began in 1969.

source.title: Resolution No. 498-25, initiating landmark designation of the Chautauqua House
source.author: San Francisco Board of Supervisors
source.publisher: City and County of San Francisco

stories.verification_notes: Board resolution read in full; names, dates and address from it. The resolution spells the founder's surname 'Casto'; Wikipedia and university archives use Costo, which is used here. Pin approximate for the 1400 block of Masonic and should be checked on the ground.

stories.title: A farmhouse among the Victorians
stories.teaser: On Piedmont Street stands the Buena Vista Farmhouse, built around the 1860s when the land was part of a dairy farm. Very few San Francisco houses predate 1870. The city began the landmark process in March 2026, calling it an early Italianate house and a rare reminder of ranching outside the city core.

source.title: Resolution No. 95-26, initiating landmark designation of the Buena Vista Farmhouse
source.author: San Francisco Board of Supervisors
source.publisher: City and County of San Francisco

stories.verification_notes: Board resolution read in full. Address 11 Piedmont Street; construction date is 'circa 1860s'. Pin approximate. Private home, view from the street.

stories.title: The houses where soldiers slept in 1906
stories.teaser: Two houses built in 1883 and 1889 at 188 and 198 Haight Street, with a barn behind on Laguna, stayed with one family until they became a landmark in 1983. In April 1906 Presidio soldiers slept in the barn, and the firestorm stopped two blocks east. Army blankets reportedly remain there.

source.title: McMorry Lagan Residence, San Francisco Landmark 164
source.author: NoeHill

stories.verification_notes: Single source (NoeHill, read Oct 22, 2026); the landmark is spelled McMorry-Lagan on NoeHill and McMorry-Lagen in some city documents. Pin approximate and near the edge of the focus area.

stories.title: The firehouse that covered the Sunset
stories.teaser: Built in 1896 at 1757 Waller Street, this wood and granite firehouse worked until 1959. From 1912 to 1956 Truck Company 12 was based here, serving a district that ran across the entire Sunset out to the Pacific. The original painted lettering still survives on the front.

source.title: Resolution No. 484-25, initiating landmark designation of Hose Company No. 30
source.author: San Francisco Board of Supervisors
source.publisher: City and County of San Francisco

stories.verification_notes: Board resolution read in full. Lettering reads Chemical 5, S.F.F.D. and Truck 12. A Fire Department museum page gives the Engine 30 company a different timeline, so only the resolution's facts are used. Pin approximate.

stories.title: The greenhouse that James Lick never built
stories.teaser: James Lick bought the pieces of two prefabricated glasshouses in 1876 for his San Jose estate, then died. A group of 27 San Franciscans bought them for the park, and the Conservatory of Flowers opened in 1879. A 1995 windstorm blew out about 30,000 panes before the 2003 reopening.

photos.caption: Floral welcome for the United Nations in front of the Conservatory
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp25.5247

photos.caption: One of the floral clock displays in front of the Conservatory
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp25.5714

photos.caption: Floral welcome to the Fraternal Order of Eagles
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.674

stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). The page says the glass came from New York around Cape Horn; the often repeated Irish origin is not in this source and is left out. Designer uncertain. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

stories.title: The windmill that watered the park
stories.teaser: Finished in 1908, the Murphy Windmill pumped groundwater to irrigate Golden Gate Park, so the city would not have to buy costly water from Spring Valley Water. Electric pumps replaced it in 1913, it fell into ruin by the 1950s, and a restoration reopened it in 2012.
stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). The page does not explain who Murphy was, so the name is not explained in the teaser. Pin approximate.

stories.title: Willis Polk's chalet and the WPA murals
stories.teaser: Willis Polk designed the Beach Chalet in 1925 as a city run restaurant with changing rooms for beachgoers. In 1936 and 1937 artist Lucien Labaudt painted a fresco of 1930s San Francisco in its lobby for the WPA. The murals remain, with a brewery upstairs.

photos.caption: The new Beach Chalet
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.5886

photos.caption: Beach Chalet
photos.credit: Philip Liborio Gangi, Richmond Review Newspaper Collection, courtesy of Paul Kozakiewicz, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp07.00140

stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Address 1000 Great Highway. Prohibition angle was not supported by the page and is left out. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

stories.title: The superintendent who lived at the park gate
stories.teaser: Built in 1896 and designed by Edward Swain, McLaren Lodge at the park's Stanyan Street entrance was park headquarters and also the home of superintendent John McLaren, who lived there until his death in 1943. It became San Francisco Landmark No. 175 in 1984.

photos.caption: The living Christmas tree in front of McLaren Lodge
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.0810

stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia); thin. Address 501 Stanyan Street. Could use a second source and a photo. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

more.title: Streetwise: Holiday Scenes in the Western Neighborhoods

stories.title: The pier that carried only water
stories.teaser: A pier stretching over 300 yards off Ocean Beach existed mainly to carry a sixteen inch intake pipe. It sent seawater to the Olympic Club's pool and the city's bathhouses, through a pumphouse near Balboa Street and a reservoir on Masonic. The system ran from 1894 until the pier's removal in 1967.
stories.verification_notes: SF Story read in full. Photos in the article come from SFMemory, the Hiller museum and others, not OpenSFHistory, so none are embedded. Pin approximate, just offshore of the pumphouse site south of Balboa.

stories.title: Last call at The Gables
stories.teaser: Eva Connett ran The Gables at 720 La Playa for 34 years and, in the late 1960s, locked the door at night to all but regulars. Across the street, Playland was closing. Last call came at 2 a.m. on Monday, May 1, 1972, and an auction of the contents followed.

photos.caption: Elevated view southeast on La Playa from Balboa, with streetcars at the Playland terminal
photos.credit: Photographer unknown, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.1730

photos.caption: Night view of Chutes at the Beach from inside the Midway
photos.credit: Laurie Hollings Photo Album, James R. Smith Collection, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp66.241

photos.caption: Demolition of Playland at the Beach
photos.credit: Greg Gaar, courtesy of Greg Gaar, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp72.7247

stories.verification_notes: SF Story read in full. The article spells her name Eva in the text and Eve in its title; Eva is used. Pin approximate for the 700 block of La Playa. Extra photo(s) added Oct 25, 2026 from the WNP Streetwise columns on outsidelands.org, using the captions and credits printed there.

stories.title: Storyland at the zoo
stories.teaser: Opened on July 25, 1959, Storyland spread Mother Goose rhymes and fairy tales over about three and a half acres at the zoo. Children paid a dime to climb inside the houses and play on the statues. Rapunzel's Castle, the last piece, was demolished on March 13, 1996.
stories.verification_notes: SF Story read in full. Photos in the article are postcards and newspaper images, so none are embedded. Pin approximate near the zoo entrance.

stories.title: Uncle Cliff of Fleishhacker Pool
stories.teaser: Hawaiian born lifeguard Cliff Kamaka worked at Fleishhacker Pool from the late 1940s until it closed in 1971, played ukulele for teenagers, and mentored the young surfers around the bonfires at Kelly's Cove. Fred Van Dyke said Cliff showed him that surfing was a way of life.
stories.verification_notes: SF Story read in full. The family photographs are courtesy of Anita Kamaka, so none are embedded; ask permission before using them. Pin is on the pool site; Kelly's Cove is a separate spot on Ocean Beach. Kamaka died in 1978.

stories.title: The roadhouses on the road to the ocean
stories.teaser: In the 1850s travelers on the road to the ocean stopped at the Lake House and the Ocean House. Joseph Leavitt opened the Ocean House in 1854 near today's Lowell High School, with a billiard salon, a bowling alley and stables for about 100 horses. A newspaper called it an assignation house on a large scale.

photos.caption: Ocean House
photos.credit: Carleton Watkins, Marilyn Blaisdell Collection, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.00812

photos.caption: Ocean Avenue west of Junipero Serra, with a painted fence advertisement
photos.credit: Photographer unknown, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.176

stories.verification_notes: SF Story read in full. The Ocean House burned in the early 1880s. Pin from the archive map point for wnp37.00812.

stories.title: The dog head on Sloat
stories.teaser: In 2001 the city restored a surviving Doggie Diner dog head and set it on a median at Sloat Boulevard and 45th Avenue. The chain, begun by Al Ross in Oakland in 1948, closed in 1986, and a grassroots rescue effort saved many of the signs. The head became Landmark No. 254 in 2006.
stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Landmark designated August 11, 2006. Pin approximate.

stories.title: The House of Mystery on the Great Highway
stories.teaser: Between Ulloa and Vicente, attorney B. S. Brooks built a seaside hotel and bar in the 1860s, nicknamed Brooks' Folly. By 1901 Alexander and Ida Russell lived there with a chapel and Japanese garden, and a 1910 newspaper story spread cult rumors. It later reopened as Tait's at the Beach and burned in 1940.

source.title: A Drive-By History of Great Highway
source.author: Nicole Meldahl

photos.caption: Tait's at the Beach at Ulloa and the Great Highway
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.946

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full. The column lists the Brooks hotel (between Ulloa and Vicente) and the Russell home (2526 Great Highway) separately; the link between them is read from its text and should be checked. Russells bought in May 1901, Ida died 1917, sold 1919, Tait's ran until 1931. Pin approximate.

stories.title: Carville, the village of old streetcars
stories.teaser: In the 1890s a Bohemian colony grew in the dunes by Ocean Beach, using surplus horsecars as clubhouses, taverns and retreats. Artists such as Xavier Martinez and Jack London spent time at Carville. It grew after the 1906 earthquake, and by the 1910s the cars were being cleared away.

source.title: A Drive-By History of Great Highway
source.author: Nicole Meldahl

photos.caption: View of Carville from the Great Highway between Judah and Irving
photos.credit: Marilyn Blaisdell Collection, courtesy of Molly Blaisdell, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp70.0816

photos.caption: Kite view of the Outer Sunset after Carville was cleared, near Irving and 48th Avenue
photos.credit: Marilyn Blaisdell Collection, courtesy of Molly Blaisdell, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp70.0282

stories.verification_notes: Great Highway column read in full; a second Streetwise column (April 2025) says a ceremonial burning of cars in 1913 marked the decline and it was mostly gone by the early 1920s, so the end date is kept loose. Pin approximate.

stories.title: The wireless telephone in the dunes
stories.teaser: At 45th Avenue and Lawton, brothers Francis and Ignatius McCarty built a shack in the dunes for their wireless telephone company. On September 2, 1905, Francis demonstrated the device from the Cliff House basement to a receiver about a mile away. He died on May 8, 1906.

source.title: A Drive-By History of Great Highway
source.author: Nicole Meldahl

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full; location is the northwest corner of 45th Avenue and Lawton. The image in the column is from the California Historical Radio Society and is not embedded. Pin approximate.

stories.title: The Union 76 at 16th and Irving
stories.teaser: For decades a neighborhood landmark stood at the southeast corner of 16th Avenue and Irving Street, a Union 76 station with an unusual structure. When it closed, supporters hoped to reuse it, but it was demolished in 2018. The column reports the site as a vacant lot behind a chain link fence.

source.title: Streetwise: Fill Er Up in the Western Neighborhoods
source.author: Frank Dunnigan

photos.caption: 16th Avenue and Irving Street
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp4.1604

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full. Vacant lot status is as of the March 2024 column and may have changed. Pin approximate.

stories.title: The Masonic temple at 9th and Judah
stories.teaser: About 2,000 people gathered at 9th Avenue and Judah Street on February 23, 1914 for the cornerstone of the Parnassus Masonic Temple. Shops filled the ground floor, with Safeway a long time tenant, and lodge rooms the upper floors. The lodge later sold the building after membership declined.

photos.caption: Parnassus Masonic Temple, southwest corner of 9th Avenue and Judah Street
photos.credit: Martin Behrman, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp4.1607

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full. Photo shows the building under maintenance around 1924. Pin approximate.

stories.title: The Irving Theatre
stories.teaser: Construction began in summer 1925 on the Irving Theatre at 1332 Irving Street, which opened in 1926 as a neighborhood movie house. It closed in July 1962 and was demolished to make room for an apartment building of the 1960s.

source.title: Streetwise: Looking Back 100 Years Ago in the Western Neighborhoods
source.author: Frank Dunnigan

photos.caption: Irving Theatre montage
photos.credit: Courtesy of Jack Tillmany, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp5.50208

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full. The cross street for 1332 Irving was not confirmed; the pin is a rough estimate on Irving Street and should be corrected on a walk.

stories.title: The first Beach Chalet, moved aside
stories.teaser: In 1925 the original Beach Chalet was moved from the west side of the Great Highway to 24th Avenue between Irving and Judah, making way for Willis Polk's new building. The Boy Scouts used it until selling in 1958, and it later burned. Reports mentioned children playing with matches in the dry grass behind it.

source.title: Streetwise: Looking Back 100 Years Ago in the Western Neighborhoods
source.author: Frank Dunnigan

photos.caption: Relocation of the original Beach Chalet
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp4.0840

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full; it points to a 2011 article by John Freeman for more. Pin placed mid block on 24th Avenue between Irving and Judah.

stories.title: The Examiner's Christmas tree on Twin Peaks
stories.teaser: In 1927 the San Francisco Examiner began building a giant lit Christmas tree on Twin Peaks, bolting hundreds of branches to a solid trunk. By 1928 a castle like archway and a shuttle bus brought crowds to Christmas Tree Point, about 900 feet up. The city later decorated a living tree at McLaren Lodge instead.

source.title: Streetwise: Holiday Scenes in the Western Neighborhoods
source.author: Frank Dunnigan

photos.caption: The Examiner Christmas tree being installed on Twin Peaks
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.5679

stories.title: Wrecks below the Cliff House
stories.teaser: Fog and rocks kept claiming ships here. The tanker Lyman Stewart was beached after a collision in October 1922, the lumber ship Coos Bay broke up on rocks north of Lincoln Park in 1927, and the freighter Ohioan ran aground near Seal Rock on October 7, 1936. Its rusted beams stayed visible until at least 1939.

source.title: Streetwise: October Happenings in the Western Neighborhoods
source.author: Frank Dunnigan

photos.caption: The SS Ohioan aground near Seal Rock, with the Sutro Baths roof at far right
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.7347

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full; it points to WNP Podcast #123. The column gives conflicting months for the Ohioan's fire and hull breakup, so those are left out. Pin approximate.

stories.title: Carzonia, a village of old streetcars
stories.teaser: After the 1906 earthquake, an emergency community at 4th Avenue and Cornwall Street used old transit vehicles as homes. Known as Carzonia, it formed in 1906 and lasted until 1910, one of the ways the Richmond sheltered people who had lost their houses.

source.title: Streetwise: Post Earthquake Scenes in the Western Neighborhoods
source.author: Frank Dunnigan

photos.caption: Carzonia
photos.credit: Helen Sjoberg Collection, courtesy of Vicky Walker, Bernal History Project, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp102.0047

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full; it links to a separate Carzonia page not yet read. Pin approximate.

stories.title: Camp 5 by the playground
stories.teaser: After the 1906 earthquake, refugees camped in Golden Gate Park near the Children's Playground at a site called Camp 5. Families first lived in Army tents before refugee cottages were built, and a photo records children from the camp posing for the camera.

source.title: Streetwise: Post Earthquake Scenes in the Western Neighborhoods
source.author: Frank Dunnigan

photos.caption: Earthquake refugee children at Camp 5, Golden Gate Park
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.1083

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full. Pin placed near the Children's Playground and offset from the Koret pin; exact camp footprint not known.

stories.title: The Memorial Museum that gave way to the de Young
stories.teaser: The Memorial Museum began as the Midwinter Fair's Fine Arts Building and showed earthquake damage to its east wall in 1906. It was repaired, then demolished in 1929 to make way for the expanded de Young Museum.

stories.title: The saber toothed tiger fountain
stories.teaser: Installed in 1924 in front of the de Young, the Rideout Fountain was funded by a bequest from Corinna Rideout. Its design shows a saber toothed tiger fighting a snake. It was in poor repair from the early 2000s, and restoration was complete by 2010.

stories.title: The Whales that left the Academy of Sciences
stories.teaser: Robert Boardman Howard's sculpture The Whales first appeared at the Golden Gate International Exposition of 1939 and 1940, and later anchored a fountain at the Academy of Sciences. When the complex was rebuilt it was removed and damaged during relocation. It waits in East Bay storage for funds and a new home.

stories.title: The fountain shaped like a cider press
stories.teaser: Thomas Shields Clark designed an apple cider press as a sculpture housing a drinking fountain for the 1894 Midwinter Fair on the Music Concourse. M. H. de Young later acquired it for the city. The metal cups were removed for sanitary reasons, and the fountain has been dry for many years.

stories.title: Monkey Island at the zoo
stories.teaser: Built in 1935 as a WPA project, Monkey Island was a fountain and waterfall habitat for more than 40 spider monkeys. The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake caused damage estimated at over 500,000 dollars. It was demolished in 1995 and the monkeys moved to a more naturalistic habitat.

stories.title: Breakfast served 24 hours
stories.teaser: Zim's Broiled Hamburgers opened in fall 1957 at the southwest corner of 19th Avenue and Taraval Street, with a bright sign promising breakfast 24 hours a day. It drew late customers from nearby theaters and bars. The chain had 12 San Francisco locations, and the last Zim's closed in 1995.
stories.verification_notes: Column read in full. The column's photo is a San Francisco Examiner image without an archive ID, so none is embedded. Pin approximate.

stories.title: Eating at Playland
stories.teaser: Playland's Great Highway strip fed the crowds with pies and fountain treats at the Whitney Brothers Pie Shop, Mexican food at the Hot House, and the IT'S IT, which the column calls the birthplace of the chocolate dipped ice cream sandwich. After Playland closed in 1972, the Hot House moved to Balboa Street until 1996.

stories.title: The cross on Mount Davidson
stories.teaser: A 40 foot wooden cross went up on Mount Davidson in 1923, followed by replacements lost to vandalism or fire. The concrete cross was lit in 1934 by President Roosevelt by telegraph from Washington. In 1997 the land sold at auction for 26,000 dollars to Armenian American organizations, who added a plaque honoring genocide victims.

stories.verification_notes: Column read in full; the concrete cross was lit March 24, 1934, and the column does not say which of the crosses the photo shows, so its date is unconfirmed. Cross is lit at Easter and on April 24. Pin placed at the summit.

stories.title: The last old hospital in the Sunset
stories.teaser: Shriners Hospital for Children opened at 1601 19th Avenue in 1923, the third site in the national network. By 1990 it was the last pre World War II hospital still operating in San Francisco. A Sacramento area replacement opened in 1997, and the five acre site was redeveloped with the main building preserved.

stories.title: San Francisco's oldest hospital, on Stanyan
stories.teaser: Founded in 1857 at First and Bryant, St. Mary's moved after the 1906 disaster to Sutter Street and then Hayes Street, and since 1972 has stood at 450 Stanyan. It is the oldest continuously operating hospital in San Francisco, and on August 1, 2024 it merged with UC.
